content: This is an updated version of a Cochrane Review originally published in 2008 and updated in 2013. Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological disorder affecting approximately 1% of the population. Around 30% of individuals with epilepsy do not respond to currently available antiepileptic drugs, with the majority of these cases being focal epilepsy. Vigabatrin is an antiepileptic medication approved for use in drug-resistant epilepsy. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of vigabatrin as an add-on therapy for individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. For this update, databases including the Cochrane Register of Studies, MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform were searched as of November 1, 2018. Additional studies were identified through reference lists and by contacting the manufacturer of vigabatrin. The review included randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials involving participants of any age with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Data were collected and analyzed using Cochrane's standard methodological procedures. The primary outcomes assessed included a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, treatment withdrawal, adverse effects, dose-response relationships, cognitive outcomes, and quality of life. Results were presented as risk ratios (RR) with 95% or 99% confidence intervals (CI). A total of 11 trials involving 756 participants aged 10 to 64 years were included. Vigabatrin doses ranged from 1 g/day to 6 g/day. All trials exhibited a risk of bias in at least three domains, including allocation concealment, blinding of outcome assessment, and incomplete outcome data. Participants receiving vigabatrin were two to three times more likely to achieve a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency compared to those receiving placebo (RR 2.60, 95% CI 1.87 to 3.63; low-certainty evidence). However, they were also three times more likely to discontinue treatment, although the certainty of this evidence was very low (RR 2.86, 95% CI 1.25 to 6.55). Adverse effects were more common in participants treated with vigabatrin compared to placebo. These included dizziness or light-headedness (RR 1.74, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.87; low-certainty evidence), fatigue (RR 1.65, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.51; low-certainty evidence), drowsiness (RR 1.70, 95% CI 1.18 to 2.44), and depression (RR 3.28, 95% CI 1.30 to 8.27). Other adverse effects, such as ataxia, nausea, abnormal vision, headache, diplopia, and nystagmus, were more frequent in the vigabatrin group, but the differences were not statistically significant, and the certainty of evidence was very low for these outcomes. Vigabatrin had minimal to no impact on cognitive outcomes or quality of life. The findings primarily apply to adults and should not be generalized to children under 10 years of age. Short-term follow-up revealed some adverse effects associated with vigabatrin use. However, longer-term observational studies have shown that vigabatrin can lead to visual field defects.
